cells.tense: You are tending what your people share, and you know it while you do it.
cells.ask: Offer one thing you know to someone who didn't ask. Then stop, and let them decide what it becomes.
cells.core:
You're the one looking after what your people hold in common — the words you all use, the way you gather, what gets passed on. Not the loudest one in the room. The one who keeps it alive. When something is fed well, you set it down and walk away, and the finish and the release come in the same motion.

That's the thing going well here, and it's worth naming plainly: care that doesn't exhaust, space held without clutching. So the next thing this balance is free to feed is bigger than one custom. Watch whether what you tend is still earning its place, or whether you're keeping it going out of habit. Either answer is useful. One keeps you honest, and the other keeps you warm.

cells.verb: tending what gets shared until it can stand on its own

cells.tense: You are shaping the shared thing toward a future it can't be handed yet.
cells.ask: Name the shared thing you're most afraid of losing. Tell one person what it gives you, with no plan attached.
cells.core:
You're on the thing your people share, but from the far side of it — planning it, defending it, keeping it alive in an argument that hasn't started. Meals, gatherings, who you all are: each one arrives already braced. Your grip is what's tiring you more than the caring is, and the grip has run ahead of where anyone actually stands.

Under the work there's the other face of this: care that doesn't exhaust, space held without clutching. That's what's here to be found. Let one thing about your group matter to you plainly, where someone can see it. Not vision, not strategy. The wonder is allowed to follow the living, not lead it.

cells.tense: You stopped offering what you know into the shared thing, and you are still holding it.
cells.ask: Bring one thing you know into a room this week. Say it once, plainly, and wait.
cells.core:
There's something you know about how your people's thing works, and you haven't said it out loud. The sharing goes on around you and you watch. Something in you stopped offering, and the knowledge stayed. So did you, on the edge of it.

You don't have to carry the whole thing to add to it. One piece, said once, into a room that's already listening. It can come out rough. What gets used will teach you more than holding onto it ever has — and being right about it isn't the point. Contact is. The watching can end with one sentence, and the room will tell you the rest.

cells.tense: You are already shaping what your people share, and you call it just how things go.
cells.ask: Pick one habit you have kept going for your people and say, once, that you did that.
cells.core:
You're already at work on the shared thing. The way your group talks, what gets repeated, what quietly stops — you've had a hand in it. But you describe it as just how things are. If it happens to anybody, it can't be yours, so it doesn't get counted.

Naming it isn't taking credit. It's putting your hands on what you're already carrying, and that's what lets you set it down later. Say it became real because it mattered to you and you kept it that way. The release grows out of finished care, and it starts with one plain sentence said out loud.

attempts.check: The draft risks claiming the person has actually been tending and handing things on across years of a shared practice, which the record does not show — the seat is where the capacity sits, not a history. A reader could fairly say they never got taken up by any tradition at all, so every cell is written so that the mechanism (tending what gets shared, or not yet touching it) still describes something in the present. The asks stay useful if the read is wrong: each is one visible act available this week regardless of whether the card is true. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line implying they were raised inside a living tradition — cut.
